title: The Lesson I Learned From Peter Warming Himself at the Enemy’s Fire
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From Peter Warming Himself at the Enemy’s Fire
(Luke 22:55)
He wasn’t warming up.
He was drifting.
“And when they had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat down among them.” — Luke 22:55
That verse hurts me every time.

Not because Peter was cold.
Because he chose the wrong fire.

Jesus was inside being mocked, questioned, and rejected.
Peter was outside, trying to survive the night without looking too much like a disciple.
And that is the lesson that cut deep into my own heart:
You can be close enough to watch Jesus… and still sit comfortably among people who do not love Him.

Peter did not deny Jesus the moment he entered the courtyard.
The fall happened in stages.

First, distance.
Then, silence.
Then, warming himself at the enemy’s fire.
Then, denial.
That is how compromise usually works.

Nobody wakes up and says, “Today I will betray the Lord.”
It starts smaller.
You stop praying with fire.
You stop standing openly for Christ.
You grow quiet where you used to be bold.
You seek comfort in places that weaken conviction.
And here’s what we miss:
Wrong fires feel good for a moment.

That fire gave Peter warmth.
It gave him cover.
It let him blend in.
But it also placed him in the atmosphere of accusation, fear, and spiritual collapse.
Some fires still burn like that today.

The fire of approval.
The fire of lust.
The fire of ambition without holiness.
The fire of ungodly friendships.
The fire of compromise dressed up as wisdom.

They warm the flesh.
But they weaken the soul.

Brother, sister—be careful where you sit when your faith is under pressure.
Be careful whose circle makes you feel safe.
Not every warm place is a holy place.
But this is not just a warning story.
This is also a grace story.

Because Peter did deny Jesus.
And Jesus still restored Peter.
That is the Gospel shining through the smoke.

Our Lord does not save perfect disciples.
He saves failing disciples who repent.
Peter fell hard, but he did not fall beyond the reach of Christ.
Jesus looked at him. Peter wept. And later, Jesus brought him back, not with condemnation, but with restoring love.
That is what sin deserves to hear and what grace actually says:

You failed.
But come back.

You got too close to the wrong fire.
But there is still room by the Savior.

Jesus went to the cross for deniers, cowards, drifters, and ashamed disciples like us.
He took our sin, our compromise, our fear, and our guilt upon Himself.
He rose again so that failure would not have the final word.
In Christ, repentance is not the end of your story.
Restoration is.
So the lesson I learned from Peter at the enemy’s fire is this:
Whatever keeps me warm but pulls me away from Jesus is too expensive.
Leave that fire.
Come back to Christ.

His presence may cost you comfort.
But His grace will save your soul.
